Delta Score Matters!
Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance in Diffusion Models

Haosen Li∗ Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Wenshuo Chen∗,‡ Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Lei Wang Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: Griffith University & Data61/CSIRO    Shaofeng Liang Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Bowen Tian Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Soning Lai Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Yutao Yue† Affiliation: ∗Equal contribution. ‡ Project Leader. †Corresponding author: yutaoyue@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract

Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in synthesizing complex static and temporal visuals, a breakthrough largely driven by Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG). However, despite its pivotal role in aligning generated content with textual prompts, standard CFG relies on a globally uniform scalar. This homogeneous amplification traps models in a well-documented ”detail-artifact dilemma”: low guidance scales fail to inject intricate semantics, while high scales inevitably cause structural degradation, color over-saturation, and temporal inconsistencies in videos. In this paper, we expose the physical root of this flaw through the lens of differential geometry. By analyzing Tweedie’s Formula, we reveal that CFG intrinsically performs a tangential linear extrapolation. Because the natural data manifold is highly curved, this uniform linear step introduces a severe orthogonal deviation. To keep the generation trajectory safely bounded, we formulate a theoretical upper bound for spatial and adaptive guidance. Based on these geometric insights, we propose Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance (SAMG), a training-free and virtually zero-cost sampling algorithm. SAMG dynamically computes point-wise conditional guidance energy, applying a conservative minimum scale to high-energy boundary regions to preserve delicate micro-textures, while deploying an aggressive maximum scale in low-energy regions to maximize semantic injection. Extensive experiments across diverse image (SD 1.5, SDXL, SD3.5 Medium) and video (CogVideoX, ModelScope) architectures demonstrate that SAMG effectively resolves the detail-artifact dilemma, achieving superior semantic alignment, structural integrity, and temporal smoothness without any computational overhead.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models have redefined the boundaries of visual generation, encompassing both text-to-image (T2I) and text-to-video (T2V) synthesis  [10, 31, 29, 16, 17, 23, 19]. They have unlocked extraordinary capabilities in generating high-fidelity, compositionally diverse, and temporally coherent visual content. The cornerstone of this generative breakthrough is Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [9], an elegantly simple yet potent conditioning mechanism. By linearly extrapolating the generative trajectory away from the unconditional prior and towards the text-driven estimate, CFG dramatically amplifies text-alignment. This operation has cemented CFG as the ubiquitous standard across modern generative architectures, seamlessly bridging classic U-Net-based frameworks (e.g., SD 1.5 [23], SDXL [19]), recent flow-matched Diffusion Transformers (e.g., SD3.5 [5]), and emerging video diffusion models.

However, despite its empirical success, the formulation of CFG harbors a fundamental flaw: it applies a globally uniform scalar across the entire spatial and temporal resolution of the latent variable. This homogeneous amplification inevitably traps models in a well-documented “detail-artifact dilemma” [24, 28]. As specifically illustrated in Figure 2 (Left) and the top row of Figure 1, the standard conditional generation often already successfully establishes the majority of fundamental structural features. To inject missing intricate semantics or force strict text alignment, users are often compelled to drastically increase the global guidance scale. Paradoxically, because this amplification is applied blindly across all regions, it inevitably destroys the local structural integrity that was already well-formed. As shown in Figure 2 (Middle) and the middle row of Figure 1, this homogeneous push strictly enforces semantic alignment but simultaneously triggers severe color over-saturation, regional over-exposure, and structural collapse. This stark contrast powerfully motivates the necessity of a spatially varying guidance strategy rather than a rigid global scalar.

To break this bottleneck, we look under the hood of the guidance evolution process through the lens of differential geometry. According to the classical Tweedie’s Formula from empirical Bayes  [8, 22], we reveal that CFG intrinsically performs an explicit tangential linear extrapolation on the estimated clean data manifold  [4]. Because the true natural visual manifold is highly curved and complex  [20], executing a uniform linear step inevitably introduces an orthogonal deviation from the manifold. This theoretical insight exposes the physical root of high-CFG artifacts: pushing homogeneously across all pixels forces high-frequency, high-energy regions (e.g., edges, micro-textures) completely off the data manifold, causing structural and temporal degradation  [4, 28].

Motivated by this geometric perspective, we formulate a theoretical upper bound for the guidance scale, proving that to keep the generation trajectory safely bounded on the manifold  [11, 3], the ideal guidance scale must not be a global scalar. Instead, it should be a dynamically modulated spatial field that is inversely proportional to the local guidance energy and manifold curvature. Since computing high-dimensional exact curvature during inference is computationally intractable and prone to numerical singularities  [30], we introduce formal mathematical relaxations—specifically, Taylor expansion and affine reparameterization  [2]—to derive a highly efficient approximation.

Based on these theoretical underpinnings, we propose Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance (SAMG), a virtually zero-cost, plug-and-play diffusion sampling method. SAMG dynamically calculates the pixel-wise conditional guidance energy ‖Δ​ϵ‖2||\Delta\epsilon||^{2} at each timestep. It applies a conservative minimum guidance scale (ωmin\omega_{\min}) to high-energy boundary regions to strictly preserve structural integrity, while deploying an aggressive maximum guidance scale (ωmax\omega_{\max}) to low-energy regions to maximize semantic injection. As demonstrated in Figure 1, SAMG resolves the detail-artifact dilemma, preserving micro-textures and temporal smoothness while ensuring high semantic alignment.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are three-fold:

  • •

    Theoretical Insight: We establish a novel geometric perspective on Classifier-Free Guidance, demonstrating that uniform tangential linear extrapolation causes manifold deviation. We mathematically formulate the theoretical upper bound for spatial-adaptive guidance.

  • •

    Methodological Innovation: We propose SAMG, a training-free, zero-cost sampling algorithm that translates the theoretical manifold constraints into a practical, pixel-wise adaptive modulation mapping applicable to images and videos.

  • •

    Empirical Superiority: Extensive experiments across static image benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic [12], DrawBench [24], MS-COCO 2017 [15], GenEval [7]) and video generation benchmarks (ChronoMagic-Bench [36]) using diverse architectures (SD 1.5 [23], SDXL [19], SD3.5 Medium [5], CogVideoX [35], and ModelScope [32]) demonstrate that SAMG significantly and consistently enhances generation quality, temporal consistency, human preference scores, and text-alignment, without incurring computational overhead.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we briefly review the fundamental concepts that form the basis of our method, specifically unifying the sampling mechanisms of standard latent diffusion models and recent flow-matching architectures, alongside the conditioning techniques used for text-driven visual generation.

2.1 Latent Diffusion and Flow Models

Generative modeling has rapidly evolved from score-based diffusion models to continuous-time flow matching. Both paradigms can be unified under the framework of transforming a simple prior distribution 𝐳T∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) into the complex data distribution 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0} via a deterministic sequence of updates in the latent space.

Standard Diffusion Models (e.g., SD 1.5, SDXL) [23, 19] gradually add Gaussian noise to the data, governed by a strictly decreasing cumulative variance schedule α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t}. A neural network, parameterized as ϵθ​(𝐳t,t)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t), is trained to predict the injected noise. During inference, deterministic samplers like Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) [29] solve the reverse probability flow to generate samples. Given a noisy latent 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}, the previous step 𝐳t−1\mathbf{z}_{t-1} is computed as:

𝐳t−1=α¯t−1​(𝐳t−1−α¯t​ϵθ​(𝐳t,t)α¯t)⏟predicted ​𝐳^0+1−α¯t−1​ϵθ​(𝐳t,t)⏟direction to ​𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\underbrace{\left(\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\right)}_{\text{predicted }\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)}_{\text{direction to }\mathbf{z}_{t}} (1)

Flow Matching Models (e.g., SD3.5, CogVideoX) [5] adopt a Rectified Flow paradigm. Instead of predicting noise, the network estimates a velocity field 𝐯θ​(𝐳t,t)\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) that transports the probability mass along linear trajectories. The sampling is performed via Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) solvers, such as the Euler method:

𝐳t−Δ​t=𝐳t−Δ​t⋅𝐯θ​(𝐳t,t)\mathbf{z}_{t-\Delta t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\Delta t\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) (2)

Despite the mathematical differences, both paradigms iteratively construct the data manifold using a predicted directional vector field. For notational simplicity and theoretical continuity, we will predominantly use ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} in our geometric formulations to represent the general neural update direction (denoting either noise or velocity), and abstract the sampling update as a generalized function Solver_Step​(⋅)\text{Solver\_Step}(\cdot).

2.2 Classifier-Free Guidance

To control the generation process using user-provided conditions cc (such as text prompts), modern architectures predominantly employ Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [9] due to its simplicity and superior semantic alignment.

CFG implicitly integrates the conditional and unconditional distributions of a generative model. During training, the conditioning signal cc is randomly dropped (replaced with a null token ∅\emptyset) with a predefined probability. This allows a single neural network to learn both the conditional estimate ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,c)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) and the unconditional estimate ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,∅)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\emptyset).

During the sampling phase, CFG modifies the model’s prediction by linearly extrapolating in the direction of the conditional prediction. The modified estimate ϵ~θ​(𝐳t,t,c)\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) is defined as:

ϵ~θ​(𝐳t,t,c)=ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,∅)+ω⋅(ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,c)−ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,∅))\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)=\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\emptyset)+\omega\cdot\Big(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\emptyset)\Big) (3)

where ω≥1\omega\geq 1 is the guidance scale. The difference term acts as an implicit classifier gradient that pushes the sample closer to the data manifold aligned with the condition cc. Crucially, the predicted noise ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,c)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) is intrinsically equivalent to the scaled conditional score function −1−α¯t​∇𝐳t​log⁡pt​(𝐳t|c)-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|c). This fundamental connection bridges the empirical CFG formulation with the geometric perspective of score matching, which we systematically explore in Section 3.

3 Methodology

While CFG significantly enhances semantic alignment in text-to-visual generation, its globally uniform scalar formulation overlooks the highly non-linear topological characteristics of the target data manifold. This results in a well-documented quality-diversity trade-off: low guidance scales fail to inject complex semantics, whereas high scales inevitably cause over-saturation and structural artifacts.

To systematically address this limitation, we re-examine the guidance evolution process through the lens of differential geometry. We formulate a theoretical upper bound for the guidance scale and propose Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance (SAMG) as a tractable, zero-cost approximation.

3.1 CFG as Tangential Extrapolation

For notational brevity, let ϵu≜ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,∅)\epsilon_{u}\triangleq\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\emptyset) and ϵc≜ϵθ​(𝐳t,t,c)\epsilon_{c}\triangleq\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c). At an arbitrary denoising timestep tt, the standard CFG modifies the predicted vector field as follows:

ϵ~ω​(𝐳t)=ϵu+ω​(ϵc−ϵu)⏟≜Δ​ϵt=ϵu+ω​Δ​ϵt\tilde{\epsilon}_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t})=\epsilon_{u}+\omega\underbrace{\big(\epsilon_{c}-\epsilon_{u}\big)}_{\triangleq\Delta\epsilon_{t}}=\epsilon_{u}+\omega\Delta\epsilon_{t} (4)

where Δ​ϵt\Delta\epsilon_{t} represents the conditional guidance direction, which we formally define as the Delta Score in this work.

To unveil the geometric significance behind this operation, we trace back to the foundational statistical principles. According to the classical Tweedie’s Formula [8, 22] from empirical Bayes, the posterior mean of the clean data 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0}, given a Gaussian-corrupted observation 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}, is strictly determined by the true marginal score function ∇𝐳t​log​pt​(𝐳t)\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t}):

𝔼⁡[𝐳0|𝐳t]=1α¯t​(𝐳t+(1−α¯t)​∇𝐳t​log⁡pt​(𝐳t))\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_{0}|\mathbf{z}_{t}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\Big(\mathbf{z}_{t}+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})\Big) (5)

In the context of score-based generative models, substituting the score field with our CFG-modified neural prediction ϵ~ω≈−1−α¯t​∇𝐳t​log⁡pt​(𝐳t)\tilde{\epsilon}_{\omega}\approx-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t}) projects the current latent state onto the estimated conditional data manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}:

𝐳^0​(ω)=𝐳t−1−α¯t​ϵ~ωα¯t=𝐳t−1−α¯t​ϵuα¯t⏟≜𝐳^0,u−ω​1−α¯tα¯t​Δ​ϵt\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}(\omega)=\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\tilde{\epsilon}_{\omega}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}=\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon_{u}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}}_{\triangleq\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0,u}}-\omega\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\Delta\epsilon_{t} (6)

Remark: For flow-based models, an analogous projection occurs during the Euler integration 𝐳t−Δ​t=𝐳t−Δ​t​(𝐯u+ω​Δ​𝐯t)\mathbf{z}_{t-\Delta t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\Delta t(\mathbf{v}_{u}+\omega\Delta\mathbf{v}_{t}), which equally acts as a linear step scaled by ω​Δ​𝐯t\omega\Delta\mathbf{v}_{t}.

Both formulations reveal a core physical mechanism: CFG intrinsically performs an explicit tangential linear extrapolation, starting from the unconditional anchor (𝐳^0,u\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0,u} or 𝐳t,u\mathbf{z}_{t,u}) and moving aggressively along the tangent space towards the direction of −Δ​ϵt-\Delta\epsilon_{t}.

To quantify the magnitude of this local guidance, we define the spatial guidance energy Et​(x)E_{t}(x) at spatial coordinate xx as the channel-wise mean of the squared difference:

Et​(x)=1C​‖Δ​ϵt​(x)‖22E_{t}(x)=\frac{1}{C}\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\|_{2}^{2} (7)

where CC is the channel dimension. This energy term intrinsically governs the effective physical extrapolation distance in the feature space during sampling.

3.2 Theoretical Bound: Manifold Deviation

Real-world natural visuals reside on a highly non-linear Riemannian manifold ℳ⊂ℝD\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} embedded within the high-dimensional latent space. Executing a linear extrapolation step along the tangent space Tx​ℳT_{x}\mathcal{M} inherently introduces an orthogonal deviation from the true manifold.

A Numerical Illustration. To concretely grasp this geometric constraint, consider the guidance vectors at two distinct spatial locations: v1=(0.1,0.2,−0.1)v_{1}=(0.1,0.2,-0.1) in a low-frequency smooth region, and v2=(1.5,3.0,−1.5)v_{2}=(1.5,3.0,-1.5) at a high-frequency texture boundary. It is worth noting that the roles of the guidance direction and the local guidance magnitude are not redundant. Although both vectors share identical optimization directions towards the text condition, their magnitudes differ drastically. Applying a fixed high scale (e.g., ω=7.0\omega=7.0) yields a moderate, safe tangential step of (0.7,1.4,−0.7)(0.7,1.4,-0.7) for v1v_{1}. However, the exact same global scalar forces a massive extrapolation step of (10.5,21.0,−10.5)(10.5,21.0,-10.5) for v2v_{2}, which inevitably overshoots the highly curved manifold boundaries. From a geometric perspective, dynamically bounding the local magnitude facilitates the model to more stably preserve crucial micro-textures without causing structural degradation.

Mathematically, at a given spatial coordinate xx, let its unconditional anchor be the starting point 𝐩∈ℝC\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} on the local data sub-manifold. Let 𝐯=−Δϵt(x)/∥Δϵt(x)∥2\mathbf{v}=-\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)/\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\|_{2} denote the normalized extrapolation direction. The ideal generation trajectory bounded safely on the manifold is described by the true geodesic curve γ⁡(s)=exp𝐩⁡(s​𝐯)\gamma(s)=\exp_{\mathbf{p}}(s\mathbf{v}), where the effective physical step size ss is governed by s=ω​1−α¯tα¯t​‖Δ​ϵt​(x)‖2=ω​1−α¯tα¯t​C⋅Et​(x)s=\omega\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\|_{2}=\omega\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\sqrt{C\cdot E_{t}(x)}. Thus, ss is directly proportional to the scaled guidance energy: s∝ω​Et​(x)s\propto\omega\sqrt{E_{t}(x)}. Standard CFG, however, strictly reaches the linearly extrapolated coordinate y=𝐩+s​𝐯y=\mathbf{p}+s\mathbf{v}. The discrepancy between yy and ℳ\mathcal{M} constitutes structural degradation.

Proposition 1 (Manifold Deviation Bound). For a sufficiently small step size ss, let κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) be the local extrinsic normal curvature along direction 𝐯\mathbf{v}, governed by the manifold’s Second Fundamental Form. The deviation error ℰd​e​v​(x)=‖y−γ⁡(s)‖2\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)=\|y-\gamma(s)\|_{2} is bounded by:

ℰd​e​v​(x)≈12​κ​(x)​s2∝12​κ​(x)​ω2​Et​(x)\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)\approx\frac{1}{2}\kappa(x)s^{2}\propto\frac{1}{2}\kappa(x)\omega^{2}E_{t}(x) (8)

To strictly bound the generation trajectory within a safe δ\delta-neighborhood of the natural visual manifold (ℰd​e​v​(x)≤δ\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)\leq\delta), the optimal pixel-wise adaptive guidance scale ωi​d​e​a​l​(x)\omega_{ideal}(x) must satisfy:

ωi​d​e​a​l​(x)≤2​δκ⁡(x)⋅ct​Et​(x)∝1κ⁡(x)​Et​(x)\omega_{ideal}(x)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\kappa(x)\cdot c_{t}E_{t}(x)}}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa(x)E_{t}(x)}} (9)

where ctc_{t} is a timestep-dependent deterministic proportionality constant (e.g., ct=C​1−α¯tα¯tc_{t}=C\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} for Tweedie projection in diffusion models, or ct=C​(Δ​t)2c_{t}=C(\Delta t)^{2} for Euler integration in flow models).

Proposition 1 formally validates our physical observation: the ideal guidance scale is not a global scalar, but a dynamically modulated spatial field inversely proportional to the square root of the local guidance energy and curvature.

3.3 SAMG: Tractable Approximation

Computing the exact high-dimensional curvature κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) during inference is computationally intractable, and the theoretical inverse square root formulation exhibits severe numerical singularities as Et​(x)→0E_{t}(x)\to 0. To derive a practical and efficient algorithm, we propose Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance (SAMG) based on two formal relaxations.

Assumption 1 (Bounded Curvature). We assume the extrinsic curvature of the natural data manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} is upper-bounded globally. Under this condition, the manifold deviation risk is dominantly governed by the local guidance energy Et​(x)E_{t}(x).

Based on Assumption 1, the optimal scale simplifies to ω∝1/Et​(x)\omega\propto 1/\sqrt{E_{t}(x)}. To bypass the singularity, we perform a first-order Taylor expansion at a non-zero local operating point η0\eta_{0}:

1Et​(x)≈1η0−12​η03/2​(Et​(x)−η0)=C1−C2⋅Et​(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{E_{t}(x)}}\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{\eta_{0}}}-\frac{1}{2\eta_{0}^{3/2}}\big(E_{t}(x)-\eta_{0}\big)=C_{1}-C_{2}\cdot E_{t}(x) (10)

where C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are positive constants. Crucially, since the target function f(E)=E−1/2f(E)=E^{-1/2} is strictly convex for E>0E>0 (its second derivative is strictly positive), its first-order Taylor expansion inherently serves as a strict global lower bound: C1−C2⋅Et(x)≤Et(x)−1/2C_{1}-C_{2}\cdot E_{t}(x)\leq E_{t}(x)^{-1/2}. This geometric property guarantees that our negative-slope linear relaxation is not merely a heuristic approximation, but a mathematically conservative boundary that strictly respects the theoretical manifold upper bound without risking over-extrapolation.

Since the exact constants C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are analytically intractable in the high-dimensional latent space, we relax this theoretical negative-slope linear boundary into a practical empirical mapping. Specifically, we introduce an Affine Reparameterization strategy operating within a predefined safety interval [ωmin,ωmax][\omega_{\min},\omega_{\max}]. We first normalize the dynamic spatial energy at step tt to E^t​(x)∈[0,1]\hat{E}_{t}(x)\in[0,1]:

E^t​(x)=Et​(x)−min⁡(Et)max⁡(Et)−min⁡(Et)+τ\hat{E}_{t}(x)=\frac{E_{t}(x)-\min(E_{t})}{\max(E_{t})-\min(E_{t})+\tau} (11)

where τ=10−8\tau=10^{-8} is for numerical stability, and the min/max\min/\max operations are performed spatially across the current timestep.

To robustly instantiate the negative-slope linear bounding derived in Equation (10), we map the normalized energy to construct the adaptive spatial guidance field 𝛀m​a​p​(x)\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{map}(x):

𝛀m​a​p​(x)=ωmax−E^t​(x)⋅(ωmax−ωmin)\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{map}(x)=\omega_{\max}-\hat{E}_{t}(x)\cdot(\omega_{\max}-\omega_{\min}) (12)

This reparameterization assigns a conservative minimum scale (ωmin\omega_{\min}) to high-energy boundary regions (E^t→1\hat{E}_{t}\to 1) to strictly preserve structural integrity, while deploying an aggressive maximum scale (ωmax\omega_{\max}) to low-energy regions (E^t→0\hat{E}_{t}\to 0) to maximize semantic injection. The final SAMG-modulated score prediction is computed point-wise as ϵ~S​A​M​G=ϵu+𝛀m​a​p​(x)⊙Δ​ϵt\tilde{\epsilon}_{SAMG}=\epsilon_{u}+\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{map}(x)\odot\Delta\epsilon_{t}. To ensure stringent geometric constraints are not diluted from high-energy boundaries to safer regions, we enforce pixel-wise independent calculations for Et​(x)E_{t}(x) without any spatial smoothing. The complete zero-cost pixel-wise sampling procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

4 Empirical Analysis

4.1 Experimental Settings

To evaluate the effectiveness of different guidance strategies, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple models, datasets, and evaluation metrics. The settings are outlined below.

Datasets.

We evaluate the text-to-image generation performance on four widely adopted benchmarks. 1) Pick-a-Pic [12]: A large-scale dataset of text-to-image prompts collected from real users, which is highly effective for evaluating human preference and diverse generation scenarios. 2) DrawBench [24]: A challenging prompt suite designed to test the fundamental capabilities of text-to-image models, including compositionality, spatial relations, and complex text comprehension. 3) GenEval [7]: An objective, rule-based evaluation benchmark specifically designed to systematically assess fine-grained compositional capabilities, such as object counting, attribute binding, and precise spatial relations. 4) MS-COCO 2017 [15]: A standard benchmark extensively used for zero-shot text-to-image evaluation. We utilize its validation set prompts to measure overall image generation quality and general text-image alignment under standard descriptive conditions. Additionally, to evaluate text-to-video generation, we utilize ChronoMagic-Bench-150 [36], a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess temporal consistency, motion naturalness, and prompt adherence in video synthesis.

Evaluation Metrics.

To provide a holistic assessment of generation quality, human preference, and text-image alignment, we employ a comprehensive suite of automated metrics. HPSv2 [33] (Human Preference Score v2) and ImageReward [34] are utilized to measure how well the generated images align with human aesthetic preferences and intent. Aesthetic Score [25] is used to evaluate the overall visual appeal and artistic quality of the outputs. To quantify the foundational image fidelity and diversity relative to the real data distribution, we compute the FID [26] (Fréchet Inception Distance). CLIP Score [21] strictly quantifies the semantic consistency between the generated images and the conditioning text prompts. Finally, we report Top-k\boldsymbol{k} Accuracy [13] (specifically Top-1, Top-5, and Top-10) to evaluate the robust success rate of the generated images being ranked as the most preferred and highly aligned outputs within candidate sets. For video generation tasks, we additionally evaluate temporal motion consistency using CHScore Flow [36], frame-level structural preservation via Frame LPIPS [37] and Frame SSIM [18], and spatial-temporal semantic alignment using CLIP SIM [21] and MTScore CLIP.

Diffusion Models & Parameters.

To demonstrate the generalization of our guidance method, we evaluate across diverse architectures. For Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD 1.5) [23] and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [19], we use 50 inference steps with a default global CFG scale [9] of 7.57.5, setting SAMG bounds [ωmin,ωmax][\omega_{\min},\omega_{\max}] to [5.0,12.0][5.0,12.0]. Notably, when evaluating FID on the COCO dataset, we lower the CFG scale to 2.02.0 and set the SAMG bounds to [1.0,3.0][1.0,3.0] with a pixel-wise independent mapping (Kernel = 1). For Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M) [5], we use 28 steps, a default CFG of 4.54.5, and SAMG bounds of [3.0,7.5][3.0,7.5]. For text-to-video generation, we evaluate CogVideoX-2B [35] and ModelScope-1.7B [32]. Both use 50 steps, a CFG of 7.57.5, and SAMG bounds of [5.0,12.0][5.0,12.0], also utilizing Kernel = 1 to prevent energy leakage.

Guidance Methods.

We compare the standard CFG [9] baseline against Perturbed Attention Guidance (PAG) [1], CFG++ [4], and CFG-Zero [6]. For PAG, we maintain the default CFG scale and empirically set its applied PAG scale to 4.5. Notably, the formulation of CFG++ operates on a distinctly different scale interval; therefore, its baseline global scale is evaluated at 0.6, and when augmented with our SAMG, its adaptive bounds are set to [0.4, 1.0].

Table 1 summarizes the performance of SAMG against baseline guidance strategies on the Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench datasets. A consistent trend across all architectures (SD 1.5, SDXL, and SD3.5-M) is that even when employing the widely accepted optimal global scales (e.g., CFG 7.5 for SD 1.5/SDXL and 4.5 for SD3.5-M), standard CFG encounters a rigid performance ceiling. At these carefully tuned baseline settings, the model struggles to further enhance semantic alignment (CLIP) without compromising structural fidelity and human preference (ImageReward). SAMG effectively breaks this bottleneck. For instance, on SDXL (DrawBench), integrating SAMG with standard CFG elevates the CLIP score to 68.33 and Top-1 accuracy to 82.63% without sacrificing aesthetic quality. Furthermore, SAMG proves highly complementary to recent advanced methods. When combined with CFG++, SAMG actively recovers the human preference degradation typically caused by CFG++’s rigid formulation (e.g., boosting the SD 1.5 ImageReward from -0.229 to -0.089), achieving near-perfect Top-5 and Top-10 accuracies while maintaining semantic rigor. The consistent gains on the recent SD3.5-M further confirm that our geometric manifold theory is architecturally agnostic.

4.2 Text-to-Image Generation

To further evaluate zero-shot generation quality and standard text-image alignment, we report the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and CLIPScore on the MS-COCO 2017 validation set (Table 2). The results demonstrate that SAMG consistently outperforms the CFG baseline across all tested architectures. Standard guidance typically forces a trade-off where higher semantic alignment degrades image quality. However, SAMG breaks this barrier, achieving lower FID scores (e.g., a significant reduction from 27.9759 to 25.4147 on SDXL) while simultaneously boosting the CLIPScore.

This indicates that our adaptive bounding strictly preserves the natural image distribution while enhancing text adherence.

Moreover, we assess the fine-grained compositional generation capabilities of our method using the GenEval benchmark (Table 2). The integration of SAMG yields comprehensive improvements across all evaluated models and granular metrics. Beyond single-object generation, SAMG exhibits particular strength in complex compositional scenarios that require precise spatial understanding and attribute isolation. For instance, on SD3.5-M, SAMG lifts the overall score from 0.63 to 0.66, with noticeable gains in challenging categories like ”Counting”, ”Position”, and ”Attribute Binding”. This structural improvement suggests that our spatially adaptive guidance effectively mitigates semantic bleeding and attribute confusion, leading to highly accurate compositional synthesis.

4.3 Text-to-Video Generation

To evaluate the generalization capability of our method across modalities and temporal extensions, we conducted a quantitative comparison on the ChronoMagic-Bench-150 dataset using two mainstream text-to-video generation models: CogVideoX-2B and ModelScope-1.7B. As shown in Table 3, SAMG consistently outperforms the standard CFG baseline across all evaluation metrics.

Semantic and Temporal Alignment.

SAMG achieves improvements in both CLIP SIM and MTScore CLIP, which measure the semantic alignment between the text prompt and the generated video. For instance, on ModelScope-1.7B, the MTScore CLIP increases from 10.56 to 10.78. This indicates that SAMG’s dynamic energy modulation is effective not only for static images but also for accurately injecting semantic information in complex, temporally-extended alignment tasks.

Frame-level Visual Quality.

Standard CFG often triggers frame-wise color over-saturation or structural artifacts during video generation. SAMG successfully mitigates this phenomenon. Quantitatively, SAMG yields a significant reduction in Frame LPIPS (e.g., dropping from 8.12 to 7.35 on ModelScope-1.7B) while simultaneously improving Frame SSIM. This demonstrates that our conservative boundary strategy effectively preserves micro-textures and structural integrity within individual video frames.

Motion Smoothness.

In terms of CHScore Flow, which evaluates the naturalness and consistency of inter-frame motion, SAMG achieves higher scores on both CogVideoX-2B (60.15 vs. 59.93) and ModelScope-1.7B (72.10 vs. 70.47). This implies that SAMG effectively prevents the manifold deviation typically caused by a globally uniform high guidance scale, resulting in smoother and more coherent transitions between frames.

In summary, as a training-free, plug-and-play sampler, SAMG not only resolves the “detail-artifact dilemma” in the image domain but also demonstrates that its core geometric manifold constraint mechanism is highly effective and seamlessly transferable to high-dimensional video generation tasks.

4.4 Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation studies on the SD 1.5 architecture (Table 4) to validate SAMG’s components: global CFG scales, adaptive boundary parameters (ωmin\omega_{\min} and ωmax\omega_{\max}), and pixel-wise independent mapping.

Impact of Global CFG Scales.

Evaluating global CFG from 5.0 to 12.0 confirms that CFG 7.5 is the optimal baseline. Forcing CFG to 12.0 slightly improves the CLIP score but significantly degrades human preference metrics (HPSv2 drops to 26.68, ImageReward to -0.010), leading to over-saturation and structural artifacts. This demonstrates that aggressively scaling standard CFG pushes latents off the natural image manifold.

Impact of Adaptive Bounds (ωmin\omega_{\min} and ωmax\omega_{\max}).

We evaluate SAMG with scale ranges of [5.0,10.0][5.0,10.0] and [5.0,12.0][5.0,12.0], both outperforming global CFG baselines. The [5.0,12.0][5.0,12.0] configuration achieves the best balance: anchoring high-frequency boundaries at ωmin=5.0\omega_{\min}=5.0 preserves structural integrity, while allowing ωmax=12.0\omega_{\max}=12.0 in smooth regions maximizes semantic injection.

Preventing Energy Leakage (Kernel Size).

To validate the necessity of strict pixel-wise independence, we compare point-wise SAMG (Kernel = 1) against a spatially smoothed variant (Kernel = 3). As shown in Table 4, spatial smoothing consistently degrades performance. Smoothing causes ”energy leakage”—blurring conservative constraints into safe regions and aggressive guidance into delicate boundaries—confirming that pixel-wise mapping is essential for accurate manifold adherence.

Collectively, these findings highlight the inherent limitations of rigid global scaling. They empirically validate that our geometrically-driven, spatially-aware guidance strategy is critical for maximizing text-image alignment without compromising the structural fidelity of the generated latents.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we identified that the globally uniform scalar formulation of Classifier-Free Guidance intrinsically causes manifold deviation, trapping diffusion models in a detail-artifact dilemma. By viewing CFG through the lens of differential geometry, we established a theoretical upper bound for spatially adaptive guidance and proposed SAMG, a training-free, virtually zero-cost sampling algorithm. SAMG dynamically modulates guidance scales based on local conditional energy, preserving delicate micro-textures and ensuring temporal consistency in videos while maximizing overall semantic alignment. Extensive empirical evaluations across both static image and video generation tasks confirm its superiority. Furthermore, by constructing geometrically sound target manifolds, integrating SAMG into distillation pipelines could fundamentally elevate the theoretical upper bound of modern CFG-free models that currently inherit teacher artifacts.

Appendix A Theoretical Extensions

In this appendix, we provide the rigorous mathematical derivations and proofs for the theoretical claims presented in the main text. Specifically, we explicitly formalize the generative sampling trajectory on a Riemannian manifold, rigorously prove the manifold deviation bound formulated in Proposition 1, establish the geometric safety of the first-order Taylor relaxation via strict convexity, and theoretically generalize our geometric constraints to continuous-time Flow Matching ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

A.1 Geometric Setup

Let the natural visual data distribution be supported on a smooth Riemannian manifold ℳ⊂ℝD\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} (D=C×H×WD=C\times H\times W), equipped with the induced Euclidean metric.

During the reverse process at timestep tt, the unconditional score prediction implicitly projects the noisy state 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} onto ℳ\mathcal{M}. We define this unguided anchor point 𝐩∈ℳ\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M} as:

𝐩≜𝐳t−1−α¯t​ϵuα¯t\mathbf{p}\triangleq\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon_{u}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}} (13)

Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) perturbs this anchor along the conditional direction. Let the Delta Score be Δ​ϵt≜ϵc−ϵu\Delta\epsilon_{t}\triangleq\epsilon_{c}-\epsilon_{u}. We define the normalized unit tangent vector 𝐯⁡(x)∈T𝐩​ℳ\mathbf{v}(x)\in T_{\mathbf{p}}\mathcal{M} and the local conditional energy Et​(x)E_{t}(x) at spatial coordinate xx as:

𝐯⁡(x)≜−Δ​ϵt​(x)‖Δ​ϵt​(x)‖2,Et​(x)≜1C​‖Δ​ϵt​(x)‖22\mathbf{v}(x)\triangleq-\frac{\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)}{\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\|_{2}},\quad E_{t}(x)\triangleq\frac{1}{C}\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\|_{2}^{2} (14)

The CFG operation structurally corresponds to a linear extrapolation in the ambient space ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}. The explicit coordinate y⁡(s)y(s) and the step size s⁡(x)s(x) evaluated along the tangent space are formulated as:

y⁡(s)=𝐩+s⁡(x)​𝐯​(x)y(s)=\mathbf{p}+s(x)\mathbf{v}(x) (15)
s⁡(x)=‖ω​1−α¯tα¯t​Δ​ϵt​(x)‖2=ω​ct​Et​(x)s(x)=\left\|\omega\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\Delta\epsilon_{t}(x)\right\|_{2}=\omega\sqrt{c_{t}E_{t}(x)} (16)

where ct≜C​1−α¯tα¯tc_{t}\triangleq C\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} is a deterministic scalar dependent on the forward schedule.

A.2 Proof of Proposition 1

Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is highly non-linear, a linear extrapolation y⁡(s)y(s) along T𝐩​ℳT_{\mathbf{p}}\mathcal{M} inherently introduces an orthogonal deviation from the true manifold. The geometrically optimal trajectory bounded on ℳ\mathcal{M} is the Riemannian geodesic γ:ℝ→ℳ\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathcal{M}, given by the exponential map γ⁡(s)=exp𝐩⁡(s​𝐯​(x))\gamma(s)=\exp_{\mathbf{p}}(s\mathbf{v}(x)).

Proposition 1. For a sufficiently small step size ss, let κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) be the normal curvature along 𝐯⁡(x)\mathbf{v}(x). The deviation error ℰd​e​v​(x)=‖y−γ⁡(s)‖2\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)=\|y-\gamma(s)\|_{2} is bounded by ℰd​e​v​(x)=12​κ​(x)​s2+𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\kappa(x)s^{2}+\mathcal{O}(s^{3}). To restrict the generation trajectory within a δ\delta-neighborhood (ℰd​e​v​(x)≤δ\mathcal{E}_{dev}(x)\leq\delta), the optimal guidance scale must satisfy ωi​d​e​a​l​(x)≤2​δκ⁡(x)​ct​Et​(x)\omega_{ideal}(x)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\kappa(x)c_{t}E_{t}(x)}}.

Proof.

By the definition of a geodesic, γ⁡(s)\gamma(s) satisfies the initial conditions γ⁡(0)=𝐩\gamma(0)=\mathbf{p} and γ˙​(0)=𝐯​(x)\dot{\gamma}(0)=\mathbf{v}(x). The second-order Taylor expansion of γ⁡(s)\gamma(s) in the ambient space ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D} is:

γ⁡(s)=γ⁡(0)+s​γ˙​(0)+s22​γ¨​(0)+𝒪⁡(s3)\gamma(s)=\gamma(0)+s\dot{\gamma}(0)+\frac{s^{2}}{2}\ddot{\gamma}(0)+\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) (17)

By the Gauss Formula for embedded sub-manifolds, the ambient acceleration γ¨​(0)\ddot{\gamma}(0) is strictly orthogonal to T𝐩​ℳT_{\mathbf{p}}\mathcal{M} and is governed entirely by the Second Fundamental Form II\mathrm{II}:

γ¨​(0)=II⁡(γ˙​(0),γ˙​(0))=II⁡(𝐯⁡(x),𝐯⁡(x))\ddot{\gamma}(0)=\mathrm{II}(\dot{\gamma}(0),\dot{\gamma}(0))=\mathrm{II}(\mathbf{v}(x),\mathbf{v}(x)) (18)

e⁡(s)\displaystyle e(s) =y⁡(s)−γ⁡(s)\displaystyle=y(s)-\gamma(s)
=(𝐩+s​𝐯​(x))−(𝐩+s​𝐯​(x)+s22​II​(𝐯⁡(x),𝐯⁡(x))+𝒪⁡(s3))\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{p}+s\mathbf{v}(x)\big)-\left(\mathbf{p}+s\mathbf{v}(x)+\frac{s^{2}}{2}\mathrm{II}(\mathbf{v}(x),\mathbf{v}(x))+\mathcal{O}(s^{3})\right)
=−s22​II​(𝐯⁡(x),𝐯⁡(x))−𝒪⁡(s3)\displaystyle=-\frac{s^{2}}{2}\mathrm{II}(\mathbf{v}(x),\mathbf{v}(x))-\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) (19)

ω2≤2​δκ⁡(x)​ct​Et​(x)⟹ωi​d​e​a​l​(x)≤2​δκ⁡(x)​ct​Et​(x)\omega^{2}\leq\frac{2\delta}{\kappa(x)c_{t}E_{t}(x)}\implies\omega_{ideal}(x)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\kappa(x)c_{t}E_{t}(x)}} (22)

A.3 Conservative Relaxation Bound

In practice, computing the exact high-dimensional curvature κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) is intractable. We relax the theoretical bound ω∝Et(x)−1/2\omega\propto E_{t}(x)^{-1/2} via a first-order Taylor expansion. We formalize that this linear relaxation constitutes a strict mathematical lower bound, ensuring geometric safety.

Supplementary Theorem 1. Let f(E)=E−1/2f(E)=E^{-1/2} represent the target boundary constraint for E∈ℝ>0E\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. Its first-order Taylor expansion g⁡(E)g(E) at any operating point η0>0\eta_{0}>0 strictly lower-bounds f⁡(E)f(E) (i.e., g⁡(E)<f⁡(E)g(E)<f(E) for all E≠η0E\neq\eta_{0}).

Proof.

The first and second derivatives of f⁡(E)f(E) are:

f′(E)=−12E−3/2,f′′(E)=34E−5/2f^{\prime}(E)=-\frac{1}{2}E^{-3/2},\quad f^{\prime\prime}(E)=\frac{3}{4}E^{-5/2} (23)

For any valid guidance energy E>0E>0, we have f′′​(E)>0f^{\prime\prime}(E)>0, confirming that f⁡(E)f(E) is strictly convex on ℝ>0\mathbb{R}_{>0}.

By Taylor’s Theorem with the Lagrange remainder, for any E>0E>0 and E≠η0E\neq\eta_{0}, there exists a ξ\xi between η0\eta_{0} and EE such that:

f⁡(E)=f⁡(η0)+f′​(η0)​(E−η0)+f′′​(ξ)2​(E−η0)2f(E)=f(\eta_{0})+f^{\prime}(\eta_{0})(E-\eta_{0})+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(\xi)}{2}(E-\eta_{0})^{2} (24)

We define the first-order approximation g⁡(E)g(E) as the tangent line at η0\eta_{0}:

g⁡(E)≜f⁡(η0)+f′​(η0)​(E−η0)=32η0−1/2⏟C1>0−12η0−3/2⏟C2>0​Eg(E)\triangleq f(\eta_{0})+f^{\prime}(\eta_{0})(E-\eta_{0})=\underbrace{\frac{3}{2}\eta_{0}^{-1/2}}_{C_{1}>0}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\eta_{0}^{-3/2}}_{C_{2}>0}E (25)

Since f′′​(ξ)>0f^{\prime\prime}(\xi)>0 and (E−η0)2>0(E-\eta_{0})^{2}>0, the remainder term is strictly positive:

f′′​(ξ)2​(E−η0)2>0\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(\xi)}{2}(E-\eta_{0})^{2}>0 (26)

Therefore, it strictly holds that:

f⁡(E)=g⁡(E)+f′′​(ξ)2​(E−η0)2⟹g⁡(E)<f⁡(E)∀E≠η0f(E)=g(E)+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(\xi)}{2}(E-\eta_{0})^{2}\implies g(E)<f(E)\quad\forall E\neq\eta_{0} (27)

This proves that the negative-slope linear function g⁡(E)=C1−C2​Eg(E)=C_{1}-C_{2}E mathematically guarantees under-approximation of f⁡(E)f(E). The practical SAMG affine mapping 𝛀m​a​p​(x)\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{map}(x) instantiates this g⁡(E)g(E) structure, providing a conservative lower bound that structurally prevents manifold over-extrapolation. ∎

A.4 Generalization to Continuous-Time Flow Matching ODEs

The geometric constraints rigorously generalize from discrete Tweedie projections to continuous-time Flow Matching and Rectified Flow frameworks. Let 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} follow the exact probability flow ODE governed by the modified velocity field 𝐯~ω\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}:

d​𝐳td​t=𝐯~ω​(𝐳t,t)=𝐯u​(𝐳t,t)+ω​Δ​𝐯​(𝐳t,t)\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)=\mathbf{v}_{u}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)+\omega\Delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) (28)

where Δ​𝐯≜𝐯c−𝐯u\Delta\mathbf{v}\triangleq\mathbf{v}_{c}-\mathbf{v}_{u}. The numerical Euler integration step is explicitly given by y=𝐳t−Δ​t​𝐯~ωy=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\Delta t\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}.

Theorem A.2 (ODE Local Truncation Deviation). Let Ψt→t−Δ​t​(𝐳t)\Psi_{t\to t-\Delta t}(\mathbf{z}_{t}) denote the exact integral curve of the vector field 𝐯~ω\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}. Let E𝐯​(x)=1C​‖Δ​𝐯​(x)‖22E_{\mathbf{v}}(x)=\frac{1}{C}\|\Delta\mathbf{v}(x)\|_{2}^{2} be the flow guidance energy. The local orthogonal manifold deviation ℰO​D​E=‖Ψt→t−Δ​t​(𝐳t)−y‖2\mathcal{E}_{ODE}=\|\Psi_{t\to t-\Delta t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})-y\|_{2} requires the continuous-time guidance scale to be bounded by:

ω⁡(x)≤1Δ​t​2​δκℱ​(x)​C​E𝐯​(x)\omega(x)\leq\frac{1}{\Delta t}\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\kappa_{\mathcal{F}}(x)CE_{\mathbf{v}}(x)}} (29)

where κℱ​(x)\kappa_{\mathcal{F}}(x) is the path curvature of the conditional vector field.

Proof.

By the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, the true solution admits the Taylor expansion:

Ψt→t−Δ​t​(𝐳t)=𝐳t−Δ​t​𝐯~ω+(Δ​t)22​d​𝐯~ωd​t−𝒪⁡((Δ​t)3)\Psi_{t\to t-\Delta t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\Delta t\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}+\frac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}}{\mathrm{d}t}-\mathcal{O}\big((\Delta t)^{3}\big) (30)

The local truncation error reduces to the acceleration norm orthogonal to the flow:

ℰO​D​E=(Δ​t)22​‖∂𝐯~ω∂t+(∇𝐳t𝐯~ω)​𝐯~ω‖2+𝒪⁡((Δ​t)3)\mathcal{E}_{ODE}=\frac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{2}\left\|\frac{\partial\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}}{\partial t}+\big(\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}\big)\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega}\right\|_{2}+\mathcal{O}\big((\Delta t)^{3}\big) (31)

Isolating the dominating quadratic guidance component for ω≫1\omega\gg 1:

ℰO​D​E≈(Δ​t)22​ω2​‖(∇𝐳tΔ​𝐯)​Δ​𝐯‖2≤12​κℱ​(x)​ω2​(Δ​t)2​‖Δ​𝐯‖22\mathcal{E}_{ODE}\approx\frac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{2}\omega^{2}\left\|\big(\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\Delta\mathbf{v}\big)\Delta\mathbf{v}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{\mathcal{F}}(x)\omega^{2}(\Delta t)^{2}\|\Delta\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2} (32)

Substituting ‖Δ​𝐯​(x)‖22=C​E𝐯​(x)\|\Delta\mathbf{v}(x)\|_{2}^{2}=CE_{\mathbf{v}}(x) and strictly enforcing the geometric safety condition ℰO​D​E≤δ\mathcal{E}_{ODE}\leq\delta yields:

12​κℱ​(x)​ω2​(Δ​t)2​C​E𝐯​(x)≤δ⟹ω⁡(x)≤2​δκℱ​(x)​C​(Δ​t)2⏟ct​E𝐯​(x)\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{\mathcal{F}}(x)\omega^{2}(\Delta t)^{2}CE_{\mathbf{v}}(x)\leq\delta\implies\omega(x)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\kappa_{\mathcal{F}}(x)\underbrace{C(\Delta t)^{2}}_{c_{t}}E_{\mathbf{v}}(x)}} (33)

This confirms mathematical isomorphism to the discrete diffusion curvature bound under the time discretization mapping ct=C​(Δ​t)2c_{t}=C(\Delta t)^{2}. ∎

A.5 Global Trajectory Deviation Accumulation Bound

We formalize how local manifold deviation errors iteratively accumulate over NN generative sampling steps to govern global structural integrity.

Theorem A.3 (Global Grönwall Error Propagation). Let 𝐳k\mathbf{z}_{k} denote the generative state at step kk. Assume the discrete update function Fk​(𝐳)=𝐳−h​ϵ~ω​(𝐳)F_{k}(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{z}-h\tilde{\epsilon}_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}) is globally LL-Lipschitz. If the local single-step orthogonal deviation is rigidly constrained point-wise such that ℰd​e​v(k)​(x)≤δ\mathcal{E}_{dev}^{(k)}(x)\leq\delta, the cumulative manifold deviation ℰg​l​o​b​a​l(N)\mathcal{E}_{global}^{(N)} after NN steps is bounded by:

ℰg​l​o​b​a​l(N)≤δL​h​(exp⁡(L​N​h)−1)\mathcal{E}_{global}^{(N)}\leq\frac{\delta}{Lh}\Big(\exp(LNh)-1\Big) (34)
Proof.

Let Πℳk​(𝐳k)=arg⁡min𝐲∈ℳk⁡‖𝐳k−𝐲‖2\Pi_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathbf{z}_{k})=\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{M}_{k}}\|\mathbf{z}_{k}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2} denote the exact projection onto the true data sub-manifold ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k}. The propagated error is ek=‖𝐳k−Πℳk​(𝐳k)‖2e_{k}=\|\mathbf{z}_{k}-\Pi_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathbf{z}_{k})\|_{2}. By the triangle inequality and the Lipschitz condition:

ek\displaystyle e_{k} ≤‖Fk−1​(𝐳k−1)−Fk−1​(Πℳk−1​(𝐳k−1))‖2+ℰd​e​v(k−1)\displaystyle\leq\left\|F_{k-1}(\mathbf{z}_{k-1})-F_{k-1}(\Pi_{\mathcal{M}_{k-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{k-1}))\right\|_{2}+\mathcal{E}_{dev}^{(k-1)}
≤(1+L​h)​‖𝐳k−1−Πℳk−1​(𝐳k−1)‖2+δ\displaystyle\leq(1+Lh)\|\mathbf{z}_{k-1}-\Pi_{\mathcal{M}_{k-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{k-1})\|_{2}+\delta
=(1+L​h)​ek−1+δ\displaystyle=(1+Lh)e_{k-1}+\delta (35)

Unrolling this recursive inequality from e0=0e_{0}=0 (perfect initialization on the Gaussian prior):

eN≤δ​∑i=0N−1(1+L​h)i=δ​(1+L​h)N−1(1+L​h)−1=δL​h​((1+L​h)N−1)e_{N}\leq\delta\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(1+Lh)^{i}=\delta\frac{(1+Lh)^{N}-1}{(1+Lh)-1}=\frac{\delta}{Lh}\Big((1+Lh)^{N}-1\Big) (36)

Applying the classical limit inequality (1+xn)n≤exp⁡(x)(1+\frac{x}{n})^{n}\leq\exp(x) for strictly positive variables:

This proves that homogeneously applying an unbounded global ω\omega induces an exponential global manifold divergence, fundamentally establishing the necessity for adaptive energy bounds. ∎

A.6 Curvature Bound via Spectral Norm of Score Jacobian

The true Riemannian normal curvature κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) relies on the intractable Second Fundamental Form. We strictly upper-bound this intrinsic curvature utilizing the spectral properties of the continuous Score Jacobian.

Lemma A.4 (Score-Hessian Isomorphism). Let ℋt​(𝐳t)=∇𝐳t2​log⁡pt​(𝐳t)\mathcal{H}_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})\\ =\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}^{2}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t}) represent the exact Hessian of the log-density. Under Tweedie’s parameterization, the Hessian is isomorphic to the Score Jacobian 𝐉ϵu\mathbf{J}_{\epsilon_{u}}:

ℋt​(𝐳t)=−11−α¯t​𝐉ϵu​(𝐳t)\mathcal{H}_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\mathbf{J}_{\epsilon_{u}}(\mathbf{z}_{t}) (38)

Theorem A.5 (Spectral Curvature Bound). The extrinsic normal curvature κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) evaluated along the guidance vector 𝐯(x)=−Δϵt/∥Δϵt∥2\mathbf{v}(x)=-{\Delta\epsilon_{t}}/{\|\Delta\epsilon_{t}\|_{2}} is strictly bounded by the local spectral norm ρ⁡(⋅)\rho(\cdot):

κ⁡(x)≤ρ​(𝐉ϵu​(x))‖ϵu​(x)‖2\kappa(x)\leq\frac{\rho\big(\mathbf{J}_{\epsilon_{u}}(x)\big)}{\|\epsilon_{u}(x)\|_{2}} (39)
Proof.

By the differential geometry of implicit surfaces, the normal curvature along a unit tangent 𝐯∈Tx​ℳ\mathbf{v}\in T_{x}\mathcal{M} of the probability level set log⁡pt​(x)=C\log p_{t}(x)=C is geometrically defined by:

κ⁡(x)=|𝐯T​ℋt​(x)​𝐯|‖∇𝐳t​log​pt​(x)‖2\kappa(x)=\frac{|\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathcal{H}_{t}(x)\mathbf{v}|}{\|\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(x)\|_{2}} (40)

Applying the Rayleigh quotient property for the symmetric matrix ℋt​(x)\mathcal{H}_{t}(x):

|𝐯T​ℋt​(x)​𝐯|≤‖ℋt​(x)‖2=ρ⁡(ℋt​(x))\left|\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathcal{H}_{t}(x)\mathbf{v}\right|\leq\|\mathcal{H}_{t}(x)\|_{2}=\rho\big(\mathcal{H}_{t}(x)\big) (41)

Substituting Lemma A.4 and the exact continuous correspondence ‖∇𝐳t​log​pt​(x)‖2=‖ϵu​(x)‖2/1−α¯t\|\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(x)\|_{2}=\|\epsilon_{u}(x)\|_{2}/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}} yields the supremum boundary condition:

κ⁡(x)≤1‖∇𝐳t​log​pt​(x)‖2​(11−α¯t​ρ​(𝐉ϵu​(x)))=ρ​(𝐉ϵu​(x))‖ϵu​(x)‖2\kappa(x)\leq\frac{1}{\|\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(x)\|_{2}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\rho\big(\mathbf{J}_{\epsilon_{u}}(x)\big)\right)=\frac{\rho\big(\mathbf{J}_{\epsilon_{u}}(x)\big)}{\|\epsilon_{u}(x)\|_{2}} (42)

This structurally bridges the manifold geometry with network parameterization, proving that delicate boundary regions exhibiting high curvature are precisely governed by large local score gradients. ∎

A.7 Sub-Optimality of Spatial Smoothing via Jensen’s Inequality

We theoretically formulate the detrimental geometric penalty of applying spatial convolutional smoothing to the energy map (formally validating the empirical necessity of Kernel = 1 in Section 4.4).

Theorem A.6 (Smoothing Manifold Violation). Let 𝒦σ​(u)\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u) be a normalized convolution kernel satisfying ∫𝒦σ​(u)​𝑑u=1\int\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u)du=1. The smoothed guidance energy is E¯t=𝒦σ∗Et\bar{E}_{t}=\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}*E_{t}. For the strict convex boundary function f(E)=E−1/2f(E)=E^{-1/2}, spatial smoothing mathematically forces the applied guidance scale to violate the theoretically safe manifold bound at local high-frequency coordinates.

Proof.

Because f′′(E)=34E−5/2>0f^{\prime\prime}(E)=\frac{3}{4}E^{-5/2}>0 for all valid E>0E>0, the constraint function f⁡(E)f(E) is strictly convex. Applying Jensen’s Inequality to the continuous spatial convolution integral:

f⁡(E¯t​(x))=f⁡(∫Ω𝒦σ​(u)​Et​(x−u)​𝑑u)≤∫Ω𝒦σ​(u)​f​(Et​(x−u))​𝑑uf\big(\bar{E}_{t}(x)\big)=f\left(\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u)E_{t}(x-u)du\right)\leq\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u)f\big(E_{t}(x-u)\big)du (43)

Consider a high-frequency spatial boundary coordinate xbx_{b}, defined as a strict local maximum of the energy field: Et​(xb)>Et​(xb−u)E_{t}(x_{b})>E_{t}(x_{b}-u) for all u≠0u\neq 0 within the kernel support. The local weighted average inherently attenuates this maximum:

E¯t​(xb)=∫Ω𝒦σ​(u)​Et​(xb−u)​𝑑u<∫Ω𝒦σ​(u)​Et​(xb)​𝑑u=Et​(xb)\bar{E}_{t}(x_{b})=\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u)E_{t}(x_{b}-u)du<\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}(u)E_{t}(x_{b})du=E_{t}(x_{b}) (44)

Since f⁡(E)f(E) is strictly monotonically decreasing, the attenuated smoothed evaluation inevitably yields an over-extrapolated scale coefficient:

E¯t​(xb)<Et​(xb)⟹f⁡(E¯t​(xb))>f⁡(Et​(xb))\bar{E}_{t}(x_{b})<E_{t}(x_{b})\implies f\big(\bar{E}_{t}(x_{b})\big)>f\big(E_{t}(x_{b})\big) (45)

Therefore, deriving the practical scale ω¯​(xb)\bar{\omega}(x_{b}) via the smoothed energy rigorously violates the upper limit ωi​d​e​a​l\omega_{ideal} derived in Proposition 1:

ω¯(xb)∝E¯t(xb)−1/2>Et(xb)−1/2∝ωi​d​e​a​l(xb)\bar{\omega}(x_{b})\propto\bar{E}_{t}(x_{b})^{-1/2}>E_{t}(x_{b})^{-1/2}\propto\omega_{ideal}(x_{b}) (46)
ω¯​(xb)>ωi​d​e​a​l​(xb)⟹ℰ¯d​e​v​(xb)>δ\bar{\omega}(x_{b})>\omega_{ideal}(x_{b})\implies\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{dev}(x_{b})>\delta (47)

This mathematically proves that point-wise independent calculations (where 𝒦0\mathcal{K}_{0} is the Dirac delta distribution) are theoretically mandated. Spatial smoothing inherently induces geometric energy leakage, forcing orthogonal manifold over-extrapolation exactly at delicate structural boundaries. ∎

Appendix B Related Work

B.1 Diffusion Models and Classifier-Free Guidance

Generative visual modeling has been fundamentally transformed by score-based diffusion processes [10, 31]. To alleviate the immense computational burden of pixel-space modeling, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [23] introduced compressed autoencoding, establishing the foundation for high-resolution text-to-image architectures like Stable Diffusion 1.5 and SDXL [19]. More recently, the field has increasingly converged towards continuous-time Flow Matching [16] and Rectified Flow [17] paradigms. These mathematical frameworks govern state-of-the-art flow-matched Diffusion Transformers like SD3.5 [5], and smoothly extend to complex text-to-video (T2V) architectures such as CogVideoX [35].

Despite these architectural advancements, aligning the generated outputs with textual prompts critically depends on conditioning mechanisms. Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [9] is the ubiquitous standard. By linearly extrapolating the generative vector field towards the conditional estimate, CFG effectively acts as an implicit classifier gradient. However, its reliance on a rigid, globally uniform scalar locks the generation into a strict trade-off: insufficient scales fail to inject complex semantics, while high scales force the generative trajectory off the natural data manifold, triggering severe over-saturation and structural collapse [24].

B.2 Mitigating the Detail-Artifact Dilemma

To alleviate the artifacts induced by high global guidance scales, numerous training-free strategies have been proposed. Value-clipping methods, such as Dynamic Thresholding [24] and CFG Rescale [14], attempt to normalize latent variance during inference to prevent over-exposure. Other approaches fundamentally intervene in the network’s feature processing: FreeU [28] re-weights the high- and low-frequency components within U-Net skip connections to balance semantics and structural details, while PAG [1] introduces an attention-perturbed self-guidance path. Recently, geometrically motivated approaches like CFG++ [4] and CFG-Zero [6] aim to regularize the tangential projection to remain bounded to the unconditional manifold.

While these methods successfully mitigate global artifacts, they apply homogeneous temporal schedules or global feature modifications, completely ignoring the highly non-uniform spatial complexity of visual data. Recognizing that distinct regions demand varying levels of semantic injection, recent works have explored spatial guidance variations. For instance, Semantic-aware CFG (S-CFG) [27] utilizes cross-attention maps to assign customized CFG scales to different semantic units. However, relying on the heuristic extraction of high-dimensional attention tensors incurs significant computational overhead. Furthermore, they are highly architecture-specific, making them challenging to deploy out-of-the-box on modern Joint Multi-Modal DiT architectures (e.g., SD3.5) where cross-attention and self-attention are intricately fused. In contrast, SAMG operates strictly on the output delta score (Δ​ϵt\Delta\epsilon_{t}), achieving spatially adaptive modulation with zero computational overhead and offering universal plug-and-play compatibility.

B.3 Geometric Perspectives on Generative Manifolds

Our methodology is deeply rooted in the geometric interpretation of generative models. Recent studies conceptualize the diffusion reverse process as evolving along a highly non-linear, curved Riemannian manifold embedded within a high-dimensional space [11, 3]. Theoretical analyses have demonstrated that employing linear tangential extrapolation in such curved spaces inherently introduces orthogonal deviation errors [4, 2]. Furthermore, through the lens of Tweedie’s Formula [8], score networks implicitly project noisy states back onto the local data sub-manifold. While previous works (e.g., CFG++) largely rely on this manifold deviation at a global level to justify modifying the unconditional anchor, SAMG takes a critical step forward. We explicitly formulate an adaptive spatial bounding mechanism based on pixel-wise curvature approximation. By translating intractable high-dimensional geometric constraints into a practical, negative-slope energy mapping, SAMG physically prevents orthogonal manifold deviation exactly at structurally delicate boundaries.

Appendix C Latent Channel-wise Energy Evolution

To further investigate the fine-grained geometric behavior of SAMG, we decouple the guidance energy Δ​ϵt\Delta\epsilon_{t} into its four constituent latent channels as defined in the SDXL VAE space. Figure 5 presents a seamless montage of these decoupled energy maps across the denoising trajectory, visualized using a thermal colormap to highlight the intensity of the Delta Score.

As illustrated, the energy distribution exhibits significant functional decoupling across channels. The Structure Channel (Ch 0) and High-Frequency Channel (Ch 3) dominate the early stages of manifold formation, where the model establishes global semantic layout and intricate micro-textures (e.g., fur patterns and sharp contours). In contrast, the Color Channels (Ch 1, 2) exhibit relatively smoother energy fields, primarily stabilizing in the intermediate steps to refine chromatic boundaries.

This inherent asymmetry reinforces our core hypothesis: a globally uniform CFG scale is sub-optimal not only spatially but also across feature dimensions. Specifically, high-frequency channels exhibiting sharp energy peaks are more susceptible to orthogonal manifold deviation, thus requiring more conservative bounding.

Future Outlook: Channel-wise Adaptive Modulation.

These observations pave the way for a more granular extension of our work—Channel-wise SAMG. By dynamically modulating the guidance scale ω\omega independently for each latent channel based on its specific frequency characteristics and curvature sensitivity, we could theoretically decouple structural preservation from semantic color injection. This would allow for an even more aggressive guidance on semantic-rich low-frequency components while maintaining absolute geometric integrity for delicate high-frequency details, further pushing the Pareto frontier of diffusion sampling.

Appendix D Limitations

While Spatial Adaptive Multi Guidance (SAMG) effectively resolves the detail-artifact dilemma in most scenarios, it encounters challenges in regions with dense semantic overlaps. Figure 6 illustrates a typical failure case involving overlapping micro-structures—specifically, an intricate earring resting against highly detailed hair.

Because SAMG modulates the guidance scale based on the spatial energy Et​(x)E_{t}(x) evaluated in the highly compressed latent space (e.g., 128×128128\times 128 for SDXL), it inherently faces a resolution bottleneck. When two distinct semantic entities with high-frequency details overlap spatially, they effectively merge into a single high-energy cluster within the local latent representation. Consequently, SAMG conservatively applies a minimum guidance scale (ωmin\omega_{\min}) to this entire cluster to prevent structural collapse.

While this defensive mechanism successfully avoids the severe color over-saturation and structural degradation seen in standard High CFG (Figure 6, Middle), it simultaneously fails to provide sufficient semantic push to distinctly disentangle the two objects. As a result, in the SAMG output (Figure 6, Right), the earring appears structurally fused with the surrounding hair strands. Future work could address this limitation by incorporating cross-attention priors to semantically disentangle overlapping high-energy regions before applying adaptive scaling.

Appendix E Detailed Experimental Setup

In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of the diffusion models, guidance strategies, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics utilized in our experiments.

E.1 Diffusion Models

Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD 1.5) [23]: A foundational text-to-image latent diffusion model that operates within a compressed autoencoded latent space. It employs a U-Net architecture to iteratively denoise latents, balancing generation fidelity with computational efficiency.

Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [19]: An advanced iteration of the latent diffusion framework featuring a significantly expanded U-Net backbone and a dual text-encoder system. SDXL is designed for high-resolution synthesis and superior complex prompt comprehension.

Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M) [5]: A state-of-the-art continuous-time generative model based on the Rectified Flow matching paradigm. It utilizes a Joint Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer architecture to transport probability mass along linear trajectories, offering enhanced semantic alignment and structural robustness.

CogVideoX-2B [35]: A large-scale text-to-video generation model that leverages a 3D causal Variational Autoencoder and an expert transformer architecture. It is specifically optimized for synthesizing temporally coherent and high-fidelity video sequences driven by textual prompts.

ModelScope-1.7B [32]: A robust video diffusion model engineered to generate complex spatio-temporal dynamics and realistic motion patterns, demonstrating strong capabilities in prompt-driven video synthesis.

E.2 Guidance Strategies

Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [9]: The ubiquitous standard for text-conditional generation. It modifies the predicted vector field by linearly extrapolating away from the unconditional prior towards the text-driven estimate, amplifying semantic alignment at the risk of structural deviation.

Perturbed Attention Guidance (PAG) [1]: A guidance mechanism that generates a degraded unconditional path by systematically perturbing the self-attention maps during the diffusion process. This provides structural guidance without requiring explicit textual null-conditions.

CFG++ [4]: A geometrically motivated variant of CFG that constrains the guidance update to remain on the unconditional data manifold, aiming to mitigate the over-saturation artifacts caused by standard tangential extrapolation.

CFG-Zero [6]: A recent guidance strategy that dynamically adjusts the unconditional prediction during the reverse process, enhancing semantic alignment and preserving sample quality without the need for additional manifold training.

E.3 Benchmarks and Datasets

Pick-a-Pic [12]: A large-scale dataset of text-to-image prompts collected from real users, which is highly effective for evaluating human preference and diverse generation scenarios.

DrawBench [24]: A challenging prompt suite designed to test the fundamental capabilities of text-to-image models, including compositionality, spatial relations, and complex text comprehension.

GenEval [7]: An objective, rule-based evaluation benchmark specifically designed to systematically assess fine-grained compositional capabilities, such as object counting, attribute binding, and precise spatial relations.

MS-COCO 2017 [15]: A standard benchmark extensively used for zero-shot text-to-image evaluation. We utilize its validation set prompts to measure overall image generation quality and general text-image alignment under standard descriptive conditions.

ChronoMagic-Bench-150 [36]: A comprehensive benchmark designed to assess temporal consistency, motion naturalness, and prompt adherence in text-to-video synthesis.

E.4 Evaluation Metrics

HPSv2 [33] and ImageReward [34]: Automated metrics trained on large-scale human feedback to measure how well the generated images align with human aesthetic preferences and intent.

Aesthetic Score [25]: Used to evaluate the overall visual appeal and artistic quality of the outputs using a pre-trained aesthetic predictor.

FID [26] (Fréchet Inception Distance): Computes the distance between feature vectors calculated for real and generated images, quantifying foundational image fidelity and diversity relative to the real data distribution.

CLIP Score [21]: Strictly quantifies the semantic consistency between the generated images (or video frames) and the conditioning text prompts.

Top-k\boldsymbol{k} Accuracy [13]: Evaluates the robust success rate of the generated images being ranked as the most preferred and highly aligned outputs within candidate sets.

Video-Specific Metrics: For temporal tasks, we evaluate motion consistency using CHScore Flow [36], frame-level structural preservation via Frame LPIPS [37] and Frame SSIM [18], and spatial-temporal semantic alignment using CLIP SIM [21] and MTScore CLIP.
